preamble.x: The Preamble states the theory of the whole Code: an ethical lawyer is a lawyer of integrity, and integrity is shown through six values that become the six Canons — independence, propriety, fidelity, competence and diligence, equality, and accountability. A lawyer serves in four capacities at once: citizen, member of the profession, officer of the court, and the client’s fiduciary.
k: Six Canons: I Independence, II Propriety, III Fidelity, IV Competence and Diligence, V Equality, VI Accountability.
Four roles of a lawyer: citizen (allegiance to the Constitution and laws), member of the profession, officer of the court, and representative of the client (fiduciary).
Breach of the Code results in sanctions; Canon VI sets the procedure and penalties.
t: Do not confuse the CPRA (2023, six Canons with numbered Sections) with the 1988 CPR (22 Canons with Rules). Citations like “Canon III, Section 6” are CPRA; “Canon 16, Rule 16.01” is the old Code.
preamble.w: The 1988 Code was rules-based. The CPRA is values-based, so that conduct not foreseen by a specific rule can still be judged against the value it offends.

i.t: CPRA, General Provisions, Sec. 1 (transitory provision)
i.s: The CPRA applies to all pending and future cases, unless the Court finds that applying it to a pending case would be unfeasible or unjust; then the 1988 Code applies.

lawyers-oath.x: The Revised Lawyer’s Oath replaces the oath in Rule 138. The new lawyer accepts practice as an honor and a responsibility, declares fealty to the Constitution, and promises to work for the rule of law, truth, justice and the rights of all persons, without discrimination, with integrity and competence.
k: Taken before admission; violating it is itself a ground for discipline.
Has a version for oaths (“So help me, God”) and one for affirmations.
t: The old oath (“I will do no falsehood… I will delay no man for money or malice”) is superseded, but cases decided under it remain good law on the duties it expressed.

gp-sec-1.x: The CPRA governs every case, pending or new, from its effectivity (May 29, 2023). The Court may apply the old 1988 Code to a pending case only if applying the CPRA would be unfeasible or would work an injustice.
t: Many 2023–2025 decisions cite the CPRA even for acts done before 2023, because of this provision.

gp-sec-2.x: Repeals the 1988 Code of Professional Responsibility, Sections 20 to 37 of Rule 138 (duties of attorneys, fees, liens, discipline grounds) and Rule 139-B (disbarment procedure), and supersedes the old Lawyer’s Oath. Inconsistent issuances and doctrines are modified accordingly.
t: Rule 138, Sec. 27 (grounds for disbarment) is among the repealed sections; grounds now come from Canon VI, Secs. 33–35.

canon-i.x: Independence means the lawyer acts free from improper influence, pressure or interference — from the client, from government, from anyone — because effective representation and the rule of law depend on it.

canon-i-sec-2.x: Win on the merits only. A lawyer may not use, or appear to use, influence over a court or agency, and may not undermine its authority.
k: Two prohibitions: exerting influence, and giving the appearance of influence.
Covers courts, tribunals and every government agency.
t: The appearance alone is enough: bragging of connections with a judge is sanctionable even if no influence was actually exerted (see also Canon II, Sec. 15).
canon-i-sec-2.o: Canon 13 (rely on the merits; refrain from impropriety that tends to influence the court)

canon-i-sec-4.x: A lawyer may not get a branch, office or officer of government to interfere in a case before a court or agency, unless a law or the court allows it.

canon-i-sec-5.x: The client decides the objectives; the lawyer, after consulting the client, decides the procedure and the means — which motions to file, which witnesses to call — and is not bound to follow a client’s instruction that is unlawful or that would compromise the lawyer’s independence.
t: Matters of procedure belong to the lawyer, but settlement, compromise and other acts that give away the client’s substantive rights need the client’s authority (Canon III, Sec. 4).

canon-ii.x: Propriety means conduct that is proper and that looks proper, in public and in private life. It is the Canon most often invoked in discipline.

canon-ii-sec-1.x: A lawyer must not engage in conduct that is unlawful, dishonest, immoral or deceitful. It applies to private conduct as well as professional work: the question is whether the act shows the lawyer unfit to be trusted with the duties of the profession.
k: Unlawful: contrary to law (a conviction is not required).
Dishonest: lying, cheating, or stealing.
Immoral: conduct so corrupt or shameless that it offends the community; disbarment needs gross immorality.
Deceitful: misleading another to his or her damage.
t: Acquittal in a criminal case does not bar discipline: the proof needed is only substantial evidence (Canon VI, Sec. 32).
Failure to pay a just debt and issuing bouncing checks have been punished under this rule.
canon-ii-sec-1.o: Rule 1.01 (no unlawful, dishonest, immoral or deceitful conduct)

canon-ii-sec-2.x: A lawyer must respect the law, the courts and agencies, their officials and staff, and the people who appear before them, and must not act in a way that reflects badly on fitness to practise or behave scandalously, in public or in private.
canon-ii-sec-2.o: Canon 11 (respect for courts) and Rule 7.03 (conduct that adversely reflects on fitness)

canon-ii-sec-3.x: A lawyer must not create or promote an unsafe or hostile environment, in or out of work, and must not commit physical, sexual, psychological or economic abuse or violence, including sexual harassment.
t: New in the CPRA: abuse and harassment are named expressly, including online.

canon-ii-sec-4.x: Use dignified, gender-fair, child- and culturally-sensitive language in pleadings, in court and online. Abusive, intemperate or offensive language is forbidden.
t: Vigorous advocacy is allowed; insults are not. Strong words in a pleading that attack the person rather than the argument are sanctioned.
canon-ii-sec-4.o: Rule 8.01 (no abusive, offensive or improper language)

i.t: Rules on the Use of Gender-Fair Language in the Judiciary, A.M. No. 21-11-25-SC
i.s: Sets the gender-fair language courts and lawyers should use in court documents and proceedings.

canon-ii-sec-8.x: Never mislead a court or agency: do not misquote or misrepresent the contents of a document, the opposing counsel’s argument, a decision or the law, and do not cite as law something that has been repealed or never existed.
t: Citing a non-existent case or a fabricated quotation — including text produced by an AI tool and not checked — falls squarely here.
canon-ii-sec-8.o: Rules 10.01 and 10.02 (no falsehood; no misquoting or misrepresenting authorities)

canon-ii-sec-11.x: A lawyer must not make false representations or statements, including in demand letters, and must correct false or inaccurate statements made in bar applications, pleadings or submissions.
t: A demand letter that threatens unfounded criminal or administrative charges to collect a civil debt is itself a violation.

canon-ii-sec-15.x: A lawyer must keep a proper distance from court and agency personnel. Familiarity that gives an appearance of influence or favor must be avoided, and claiming influence is forbidden.

canon-ii-sec-17.x: No soliciting legal business, directly or indirectly. Advertising is allowed only if dignified, verifiable and factual (biographical data, contact details, fields of practice, services) and never self-laudatory. No paying media, award-giving bodies or personalities for publicity.
k: Solicitation: prohibited outright.
Advertising: allowed within limits — dignified, verifiable, factual, not self-laudatory, any platform.
Paying for publicity or awards: prohibited.
t: The 1988 Code allowed only a narrow list of ads (Rule 3.01, 2.03). The CPRA is more liberal on platforms but keeps the ban on self-praise and on paid publicity.

d.h: A lawyer who used agents to approach seafarers and persuade them to transfer their cases to him was suspended. Soliciting through others is still solicitation, and law is a profession, not a trade.

canon-ii-sec-19.x: Sub judice rule: while a case is pending, a lawyer must not make public statements that would prejudge it, sway public opinion, or obstruct the administration of justice.

canon-ii-sec-29.x: A lawyer who left government may not accept engagement in any matter in which he or she intervened while in government service.
t: The bar is tied to the specific “matter” handled in government, not to every case against the former agency.
Read with Sec. 7(b) of RA 6713 (one-year bar on private practice connected with one’s former office).

i.t: RA 6713, Sec. 7(b)
i.s: Public officials may not practise their profession in connection with their former office for one year after leaving it.

d.h: A former Solicitor General who, while in office, advised on the liquidation of a bank was not barred from later representing parties in sequestration cases: the “matter” he handled was the liquidation, not the sequestration, and the rule is not applied to bar lawyers indefinitely.
d.r: Defines “matter” and “intervention” under the revolving-door rule.

canon-ii-sec-34.x: Lawyers may use paralegals for non-diagnostic, non-advisory legal work, but must direct and supervise them, and the duty of confidentiality extends to the paralegal.

canon-ii-sec-35.x: Some tasks belong to lawyers alone. A lawyer may not let a non-lawyer, including a paralegal, accept cases for the lawyer, give legal advice or opinions, act without the lawyer’s supervision, hold himself or herself out as a lawyer, appear in court or formal proceedings for a client (unless the law or rules allow), negotiate with third parties without supervision, sign correspondence containing a legal opinion, or do anything only lawyers may do.
t: Law student practitioners under Rule 138-A are outside this prohibition.

i.t: Revised Law Student Practice Rule (Rule 138-A) and the Clinical Legal Education Program, A.M. No. 19-03-24-SC
i.s: Lets certified law students appear and give limited legal services under a supervising lawyer through a law school’s clinic; the clinic director and supervising lawyer answer for the students’ work.

canon-ii-sec-36.x: A lawyer who uses social media must understand its benefits and risks and use it responsibly, consistent with the Code.
t: Sections 36 to 44 form a chapter on social media, new in the CPRA.

canon-ii-sec-38.x: A lawyer must not knowingly or maliciously post, share or upload false or unverified statements or disinformation.

canon-ii-sec-40.x: Do not reveal privileged information in online posts, even in a “private” group.

canon-ii-sec-42.x: A lawyer must not use social media to communicate with a judge, justice or agency officer about a pending case in order to influence its outcome.

canon-ii-sec-43.x: A lawyer may post general legal information online. But advice on specific facts disclosed by a person online is Limited Legal Service, and it creates duties (confidentiality and conflict-of-interest rules apply).
t: General information creates no lawyer-client relationship; specific advice can.

canon-iii.x: Fidelity is loyalty: to the Constitution and laws, to the administration of justice as an officer of the court, and to the client within the bounds of law. It is the longest Canon and covers the lawyer-client relationship from start to end, conflicts, confidentiality, fees and money.

canon-iii-sec-1.x: Practice of law: rendering legal service or doing acts that apply law, legal principles, procedure or legal knowledge, which require the skill of a lawyer — in or out of court.
t: It is not limited to court appearances: preparing contracts, giving legal advice and similar work count.

d.h: Practice of law means any activity, in or out of court, that requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience. Monsod’s work as a lawyer-economist, manager and negotiator counted toward the ten years of practice required of the COMELEC Chairman.
d.r: The standard definition, now written into the CPRA.

canon-iii-sec-2.x: The responsible lawyer upholds the Constitution and laws, promotes respect for legal processes, assists in the speedy administration of justice as an officer of the court, and represents the client with zeal within the bounds of the law and the CPRA.

canon-iii-sec-3.x: The lawyer-client relationship is of the highest fiduciary character. It begins when the lawyer agrees, expressly or impliedly, to render legal service, and duties of confidentiality may attach even to a prospective client.
t: No written contract or fee is needed for the relationship to exist; consultation with a view to engagement can be enough.

canon-iii-sec-4.x: A lawyer binds the client in a legal engagement only when authorized in writing.
t: Compromise of the client’s claim needs special authority.

canon-iii-sec-6.x: A lawyer must honor the trust the client reposes: no abuse or exploitation of the relationship. Money received for a purpose must be used for it or returned on demand.
t: Failure to return money on demand gives rise to a presumption of misappropriation.

canon-iii-sec-7.x: No frivolous suits or abuse of court processes: no filing of suits without basis in law and evidence, no undue delay of executing a valid judgment, no abuse of procedure.

canon-iii-sec-8.x: Encourage the client to avoid, end or settle disputes on fair terms, and help the parties and the court with mediation and other dispute resolution.

canon-iii-sec-13.x: A lawyer may not represent conflicting interests unless all concerned give written informed consent after full disclosure. The test: is it the lawyer’s duty to fight for an issue or claim for one client that he or she must oppose for the other?
k: Conflict exists when a lawyer represents inconsistent or opposing interests of two or more persons.
Cure: written informed consent of all concerned, after full disclosure.
The test looks at duties, not at whether confidences were actually used.
t: It does not matter that the cases are unrelated or that no confidential information was actually used: the duty to the client continues.
Consent must be written and informed; oral consent is not enough under the CPRA.

d.h: A lawyer who acted for a corporation’s board and then appeared for the directors in a derivative suit against them by shareholders represented conflicting interests. The Court explained the tests: whether one duty requires opposing what the other requires; whether acceptance of the new engagement will require the lawyer to use against the former client information obtained in the previous relation.
d.r: The tests for conflict of interest, now restated in Sec. 13.

canon-iii-sec-14.x: Rules for dealings with current clients that create conflicts. A lawyer may not enter into a business transaction with a client, or acquire an interest adverse to the client, unless the terms are fair and fully disclosed in writing, the client is advised in writing to consult an independent lawyer, and the client gives written informed consent. The section lists further situations of the same kind.
k: Business deal with a client: (1) fair and fully disclosed in writing; (2) written advice to seek independent counsel; (3) written informed consent to the terms and to the lawyer’s role.
t: All three conditions are needed; a client’s signature on the deal alone is not enough.

canon-iii-sec-16.x: A lawyer must not have dating, romantic or sexual relations with a client during the engagement, unless the relationship existed before the engagement.
t: New in the CPRA.

canon-iii-sec-17.x: Conflict with a former client: a lawyer may not act against a former client in the same or a related matter, or use information from the former engagement against that client, without written informed consent.

canon-iii-sec-21.x: Government lawyers and conflicts: a lawyer in government service must not represent private interests that conflict with the government’s, and must observe the rules on private practice.

i.t: RA 6713, Sec. 7
i.s: Prohibited acts of public officials, including private practice unless authorized and not in conflict with official functions.

canon-iii-sec-22.x: A conflict of interest of a Public Attorney’s Office lawyer is imputed only to that lawyer and his or her direct supervisor. Other PAO lawyers may still represent the affected client after full disclosure and written informed consent.
t: The PAO asked the Court to delete this section; the Court refused (A.M. No. 23-05-05-SC, 2023) and later held the PAO chief in contempt over an office order that resisted it (2024).

d.n: Request of the Public Attorney’s Office to Delete Section 22, Canon III of the Proposed CPRA
d.h: The Court denied the request, holding that the rule protects the poor’s access to counsel: imputing a conflict to the whole PAO would leave one of two indigent parties without a lawyer.
d.r: Explains why this section departs from the usual rule that a conflict is imputed to all lawyers of a firm.

canon-iii-sec-27.x: A lawyer must keep the client’s confidences and respect data privacy laws. The duty continues after the engagement ends.
t: The duty survives the end of the engagement.
Read with the Data Privacy Act (RA 10173): client data are personal information the lawyer must protect.

i.t: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173)
i.s: Personal and sensitive personal information of clients must be processed lawfully and kept secure.

d.h: Lawyers could not be compelled to disclose the identity of the clients for whom they set up corporations: where revealing the name would expose the client to the very liability that was the subject of the legal advice, the identity itself is privileged.
d.r: The leading case on when a client’s identity is privileged.

canon-iii-sec-28.x: Protect client confidences from disclosure by the lawyer and by the lawyer’s staff and associates.

canon-iii-sec-35.x: Limited Legal Services: short-term, discrete legal help (advice, document review) without an expectation of continuing representation. Conflict and confidentiality rules still apply.
t: New in the CPRA.

canon-iii-sec-41.x: Fees must be fair and reasonable, judged by the factors the section lists: time spent and extent of service; novelty and difficulty of the issues; skill and expertise required; probability of losing other engagements; customary charges and the IBP chapter’s schedule of fees; the value of the client’s interest or the benefit to the client; contingency or certainty of compensation; and the character of the engagement, among others.
k: Without a written agreement, fees are fixed on quantum meruit (as much as the lawyer deserves).
A contingent fee is allowed if reasonable and not unconscionable.
t: Courts may reduce an unconscionable fee even if the client agreed to it.

canon-iii-sec-43.x: A lawyer may not share, split or divide a fee for legal services — directly or indirectly — with anyone not licensed or authorized to practise law.

canon-iii-sec-47.x: Attorney’s liens: a retaining lien over the client’s funds, documents and papers in the lawyer’s lawful possession, and a charging lien over money judgments the lawyer secured, to answer for unpaid fees.

canon-iii-sec-49.x: A lawyer must account for all money and property received from or for the client, and must deliver them when due or on demand.

canon-iii-sec-50.x: Keep the client’s funds separate from the lawyer’s own; no commingling.

canon-iii-sec-51.x: A lawyer may not acquire an interest in the subject of the litigation he or she is handling.
t: Read with Art. 1491(5) of the Civil Code, which forbids lawyers to buy property in litigation in which they take part.

canon-iii-sec-52.x: While the engagement lasts, a lawyer may not lend money to a client except in urgent and justifiable circumstances (advances for fees and necessary expenses of the case are not covered), and may not borrow from a client unless the client’s interests are fully protected by the nature of the case or by independent advice.
t: Borrowing is allowed for ordinary commercial transactions the client offers to the public, an existing business relationship, or a contract between them.

canon-iii-sec-53.x: A lawyer may end the engagement only for good cause and with written notice. The grounds listed: the client pursues an illegal or immoral course; the client insists on conduct that violates the Code; inability to work with co-counsel harms the client; the lawyer’s condition makes the work difficult; the client deliberately fails to pay or comply with the retainer, or cannot be found; the lawyer is elected or appointed to public office; and similar cases.
t: Written notice is required; abandoning the client without it is a violation even if a ground exists.

canon-iii-sec-54.x: The client may end the engagement at any time, with or without cause, but must pay the fees earned.

canon-iv.x: A lawyer must bring competence, diligence, commitment and skill to every engagement, and keep learning.

canon-iv-sec-1.x: Provide legal service that is competent, efficient and conscientious.

canon-iv-sec-3.x: Act on the client’s matter diligently and on time, and be punctual in every appearance and filing.
t: Missing a deadline to appeal or failing to file a required brief is the classic violation; it is not excused by heavy workload.

canon-iv-sec-6.x: Keep the client regularly informed of the status and result of the matter, and respond to the client’s requests for information.

canon-iv-sec-8.x: A competent lawyer keeps learning throughout his or her career.

i.t: Mandatory Continuing Legal Education, B.M. No. 850, as amended
i.s: Every practising lawyer must complete the required MCLE units each compliance period; non-compliance makes the lawyer a delinquent member and pleadings must state the MCLE compliance number.

canon-v.x: Every person is entitled to legal representation, without discrimination, and lawyers owe a higher standard of care to the vulnerable.

canon-v-sec-1.x: A lawyer may not refuse to represent a person solely because of nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity, religion, disability, age, or similar grounds.

canon-v-sec-3.x: A lawyer may not refuse an indigent person except when (a) he or she cannot do the work competently for a justifiable cause, (b) there would be a conflict of interest, or (c) the lawyer is related to the adverse party or counsel within the degrees stated.
k: Indigent: no money or property sufficient for food, shelter and basic necessities for oneself and family.

i.t: Rules on the Unified Legal Aid Service (ULAS), A.M. No. 22-11-01-SC (in force February 3, 2025)
i.s: Requires every lawyer to render free legal aid each compliance period (or pay in lieu where allowed), and organizes legal aid through the IBP and accredited providers. It replaced the 2009 Rule on Mandatory Legal Aid Service (B.M. No. 2012).

canon-vi.x: By taking the oath a lawyer accepts accountability to society, the courts, the profession and clients. Canon VI is the procedure and the penalties.

canon-vi-sec-1.x: Disciplinary proceedings are confidential and summary in nature, but the Supreme Court’s final order is published like any decision.
t: They are sui generis: neither civil nor criminal. Their object is to protect the courts and the public, not to punish the lawyer.

d.h: Disciplinary proceedings against lawyers are sui generis: an investigation by the Court into the conduct of its own officers, not a civil or criminal action. The lawyer was suspended for scurrilous attacks on the Court.
d.r: The classic statement of the nature of disciplinary proceedings.

canon-vi-sec-2.x: Proceedings may start on the Supreme Court’s own initiative, or on a verified complaint filed with the Supreme Court or with the IBP. Complaints against sitting Justices of the appellate courts and judges go to the Supreme Court.

canon-vi-sec-16.x: The complainant’s desistance, settlement or withdrawal does not end the case: the Court may proceed if the evidence supports it.
t: A favorite trap: an affidavit of desistance does not bar discipline.

canon-vi-sec-32.x: The complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence — relevant evidence a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.
t: Not proof beyond reasonable doubt, and not preponderance. An acquittal does not bar discipline; a conviction is not required.

canon-vi-sec-33.x: Serious offenses include gross misconduct; serious dishonesty, fraud or deceit (including falsification and untruthful statements); bribery or corruption; gross negligence that deprives the client of his or her day in court; conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude; grossly immoral conduct; misappropriating a client’s funds or property; gross ignorance of the law attended by bad faith or malice; and the other acts listed.
t: Penalties for serious offenses are in Sec. 37(a): disbarment, suspension over six months, revocation of notarial commission, or a fine over P100,000.

canon-vi-sec-37.x: Penalties by class of offense. Serious: disbarment; suspension over six months; revocation of notarial commission with disqualification for at least two years; or a fine over P100,000. Less serious: suspension of one to six months (or revocation of notarial commission with disqualification under two years) and/or a fine of P35,000 to P100,000. Light: fine of P1,000 to P35,000, censure or reprimand, plus possible community or legal aid service.
k: Money or property owed to the client in connection with the engagement must always be ordered returned.
t: Sanctions may be combined for serious and less serious offenses.
Read with Secs. 38–40: modifying circumstances can double the maximum or halve the minimum, and separate penalties are imposed for separate acts.

canon-vi-sec-38.x: Mitigating circumstances (first offense, good faith, restitution, remorse, reconciliation, and others) and aggravating circumstances (prior liability, fraudulent concealment, bad faith, lack of remorse, defiance of Court or IBP orders, and others) adjust the penalty.
t: Age and years in practice appear in both lists: they can cut either way.

canon-vi-sec-39.x: With only aggravating circumstances, the Court may double the maximum suspension or fine, or disbar. With only mitigating circumstances, it may go down to half the minimum. When both exist, they may offset.

canon-vi-sec-40.x: Separate acts, separate penalties; if they add up to more than five years’ suspension or P1,000,000 in fines, the Court may disbar instead. One act that is several offenses gets only the penalty for the most serious.

canon-vi-sec-43.x: The Court’s decision imposing discipline is immediately executory.
t: A motion for reconsideration does not stay the suspension.

canon-vi-sec-45.x: After a suspension ends, the lawyer files a sworn statement that he or she did not practise during the suspension; it is proof of compliance and lets the lawyer resume practice. A false statement is a ground for disbarment.

canon-vi-sec-47.x: A disbarred lawyer may seek reinstatement through a verified petition for judicial clemency, but only after five years from receipt of the disbarment decision.
t: The five-year wait is new and strict.

canon-vi-sec-48.x: The petition for clemency must show: filing after five years; full compliance with prior orders; recognition of the wrong and genuine reform; reconciliation or a good-faith attempt (or a public apology where there is no private offended party); and present good moral character and fitness. It may add that the lawyer still has productive years or shows promise.
t: These conditions codify the clemency guidelines first laid down in Re: Letter of Judge Augustus C. Diaz, A.M. No. 07-7-17-SC (2007).

canon-vi-sec-52.x: A disbarred or suspended lawyer may not practise in any form: no legal advice, no appearance before courts or agencies, no representation at depositions, no negotiating for clients, no handling of client funds, no teaching law subjects, and no notarial work. A suspended lawyer must stop at once; clients may hire new counsel.
t: Teaching law subjects and notarial work are expressly covered — both are common exam traps.

canon-i-sec-1.x: The opening duty of the whole Code: make legal services accessible, and deliver them efficiently and effectively — while staying independent and acting with integrity. Access and independence are paired on purpose: a lawyer who is easy to reach but beholden to someone is not serving justice.
k: Three things at once: accessibility, independence, integrity.
The aim is the efficient and effective delivery of justice, not only of a service to one client.
canon-i-sec-1.o: Canon 2 (making legal services available in an efficient and convenient manner)

canon-i-sec-3.x: In arguing a client’s cause, a lawyer must not be swayed by dishonest or immoral considerations, or by outside influence or pressure — from the client, the public, the media, or anyone else.
t: Pressure from the lawyer’s own client is still “pressure”: independence runs against the client too (see Sec. 5, the client may not dictate procedure).

canon-ii-sec-5.x: In everything, personal or professional, the lawyer insists on fairness and obedience to the law — including with his or her own client.

canon-ii-sec-6.x: No harassing or threatening another lawyer, that lawyer’s client, a witness, or any court or agency official or employee.
t: A threat that amounts to a crime is a serious offense (Sec. 33(m)); other unlawful threats are less serious (Sec. 34(h)).

canon-ii-sec-7.x: Formal decorum before every court and agency. Attire must fit the dignity of the forum, with respect for the lawyer’s sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression.
t: The SOGIE clause is new: the dress rule may not be used to force a lawyer to dress against his or her gender identity or expression.

canon-ii-sec-9.x: Two prohibitions: do not block another lawyer’s access to evidence (testimonial evidence included) during trial; and never alter, destroy or conceal evidence.
t: Hiding a witness is “obstructing access to testimonial evidence”.

canon-ii-sec-10.x: Rules for handling witnesses: no impropriety in presenting or confronting them; no coaching, abuse, discrimination or harassment, in or out of court; no talking to a witness during a break while the witness is still under examination; and no helping a witness lie.
k: Coaching is barred — preparing a witness to tell the truth clearly is not coaching; feeding answers is.
The recess rule: once examination has begun and until it ends, the lawyer may not speak with the witness during breaks.
No directing, assisting or abetting a witness’s misrepresentation.
t: The recess rule applies to one’s own witness too.

canon-ii-sec-12.x: Two reporting duties. First, tell the court or agency at once of dishonest, deceitful or misleading conduct connected with a matter the lawyer is handling there. Second, report transactions the law requires to be reported — e.g., covered and suspicious transactions under anti-money-laundering law. Reporting these is not a breach of confidentiality, the information stays confidential, and a baseless report exposes the reporter to civil, criminal or administrative action.
k: Duty 1: candor to the tribunal about deceit in the lawyer’s own matter.
Duty 2: statutory reporting (AMLA and similar).
Safe harbor: lawful reports do not violate confidentiality.
Counterweight: baseless reports are actionable.
t: Read with the AMLA: a lawyer is a covered person only for listed services (managing client assets, setting up companies, and the like), and the AMLA itself excludes information protected by legal professional privilege.

i.t: Anti-Money Laundering Act (R.A. No. 9160), as amended — lawyers as covered persons since R.A. No. 10365 (2013)
i.s: Lawyers who, for a client, manage money or assets, organize contributions for companies, create or manage juridical persons, or buy and sell business entities are covered persons who must report covered and suspicious transactions. The law itself spares information obtained under professional secrecy or legal professional privilege.

canon-ii-sec-13.x: No accusing another lawyer — directly or through others — of misconduct, impropriety or a crime without factual or legal basis, and no filing (or helping file) frivolous or baseless complaints against another lawyer.
t: Instituting frivolous actions, once a final decision so finds, is a less serious offense (Sec. 34(i)).
canon-ii-sec-13.o: Canon 8 (courtesy, fairness and candor toward colleagues)

canon-ii-sec-14.x: Grievances against a judge or other officer go through the proper remedy before the proper authority — not to the media or social media. Insinuating improper motive without substantial evidence is itself a ground for discipline.
t: The standard is “substantial evidence”: a suspicion is not enough to say a judge was bribed or biased.

canon-ii-sec-16.x: A lawyer who reasonably believes a life-threatening situation is likely to develop in connection with any proceeding must report it immediately to the proper authorities.
canon-ii-sec-16.w: Courtroom violence against judges, lawyers and witnesses is a real risk; a lawyer often hears of it first.

canon-ii-sec-18.x: After a case or matter ends, the lawyer may not make public appearances or statements about it to promote himself or herself, to self-aggrandize, or to win public sympathy.
t: Sub judice (Sec. 19) covers pending cases; Sec. 18 covers terminated ones — the motive (self-promotion) is what is banned, not all discussion.

canon-ii-sec-20.x: At the first chance, the lawyer must formally disclose on the record any relationship or connection with the judge, presiding officer or court personnel — or between them and the lawyer’s partners, associates or clients — that could be a ground for mandatory inhibition.
t: Disclosure must be formal and on record — telling the judge privately is not compliance.

i.t: Rule 137, Sec. 1 of the Rules of Court (disqualification of judges)
i.s: A judge must not sit where he or she is related to a party within the sixth degree, or to counsel within the fourth degree, of consanguinity or affinity, among other grounds. Sec. 20 makes the lawyer flag such a relationship early.

canon-ii-sec-21.x: No gifts, donations or contributions of any value, on any occasion, to any court or agency or its officers and staff — directly or indirectly.
t: “Any value” and “any occasion”: Christmas gifts to court staff are covered. There is no de minimis exception in the text.

canon-ii-sec-22.x: A lawyer must not exploit a non-lawyer’s lack of education or legal knowledge.
canon-ii-sec-22.w: The lawyer’s superior knowledge is a public trust; using it against the uninformed (for example, in a deal with an unrepresented person) is the abuse the rule targets.

canon-ii-sec-23.x: Two rules on abuse of process. Forum shopping — done knowingly or through gross negligence — is banned as a falsehood imposed on the courts. And no filing (or advising) multiple cases to gain leverage, harass, delay, or raise the cost of litigation.
k: Forum shopping: filing actions involving the same parties, rights and reliefs in different fora, hoping for a favorable result (tested by litis pendentia or res judicata).
Multiple suits as a weapon — even if not technically forum shopping — are separately banned.
t: Willful forum shopping, and forum shopping through gross negligence, are serious offenses (Sec. 33(n)).
canon-ii-sec-23.o: Rule 12.02 (no multiple actions from the same cause) and Rule 12.04

canon-ii-sec-24.x: No encroaching on another lawyer’s engagement. This includes communicating, negotiating or dealing with a person who has a lawyer, unless the person initiated it or the other lawyer knows. But anyone seeking relief against a perceived unfaithful or neglectful counsel may be properly advised.
k: The “no-contact” rule: deal with a represented party through his or her lawyer.
Two exceptions: the represented person initiates, or the person’s lawyer knows.
Advising someone unhappy with counsel is allowed.

d.h: A lawyer whose agent persuaded another lawyer’s clients to transfer their cases to him was suspended, among others, for encroaching on that lawyer’s professional employment.
d.r: Encroachment by inducing clients to switch.

canon-ii-sec-25.x: A solo practitioner has no partner to catch what falls through: he or she must make sure every matter that needs a lawyer’s skill and judgment is handled promptly and competently.

canon-ii-sec-26.x: A law firm is an office, partnership or association made up only of lawyers practising law and holding themselves out as such. Its name may not be false, misleading or assumed. A deceased, incapacitated or retired partner’s name may stay, if the firm says so in all its communications.
t: Only lawyers: a firm with non-lawyer partners is not a law firm under the CPRA.
The 1988 rule allowed only a deceased partner’s name; the CPRA adds incapacitated and retired partners.

d.n: In re: Petition for Authority to Continue Use of the Firm Name “Sycip, Salazar, Feliciano, Hernandez & Castillo”
d.h: The Court then refused to let firms keep the names of deceased partners: a firm name should identify the lawyers who actually practise in it, and a partnership for the practice of law is not a business that can trade on a name.
d.r: The old rule — later relaxed by Rule 3.02 (1988) and Sec. 26 (2023).

canon-ii-sec-27.x: A partner who takes public office must withdraw from the firm, and his or her name must come off the firm name — unless the law allows that office to practise law at the same time.
canon-ii-sec-27.w: So that the firm does not trade on the influence of an official who is not practising with it.

canon-ii-sec-28.x: Government lawyers answer to the CPRA, to R.A. No. 6713, and to other laws on public officers. Discipline under the CPRA is separate from any liability under those other laws.
t: Separate and distinct: an Ombudsman or Civil Service ruling does not bar — and is not required for — discipline as a lawyer. (But see Canon VI, Sec. 2: such complaints are filed only with the Supreme Court.)

i.t: R.A. No. 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, 1989)
i.s: Section 7 prohibits, among others, a financial or material interest in any transaction requiring the approval of one’s office, and soliciting or accepting gifts in connection with official duties.

canon-ii-sec-30.x: A government lawyer may not use office to advance his or her own or another’s private or financial interest in transactions the office must approve, may not solicit or take anything of value in connection with it, and may not give anything of value to or unduly favor people dealing with the office in expectation of a return.

i.t: R.A. No. 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, 1989)
i.s: Section 7 prohibits, among others, a financial or material interest in any transaction requiring the approval of one’s office, and soliciting or accepting gifts in connection with official duties.

canon-ii-sec-31.x: A public prosecutor’s first duty is not to convict but to see justice done. Suppressing facts, hiding or tampering with evidence, coaching a witness or offering false testimony is ground for discipline. Private lawyers authorized to prosecute under the prosecutor’s direct supervision carry the same duties.
k: The prosecutor represents the State, whose interest is justice — including the acquittal of the innocent.
Applies to authorized private prosecutors too.

d.h: The Court described the prosecutor as the representative of a sovereignty whose interest in a criminal prosecution is not that it shall win a case but that justice shall be done — borrowing the classic formulation of the U.S. Supreme Court in Berger v. United States (1935).
d.r: The source of the “not to convict” formula.

canon-ii-sec-32.x: Law deans, administrators and teachers are held to the full CPRA standards — propriety, respectability and decorum inside and outside the classroom, and in all media.

canon-ii-sec-33.x: A law teacher or school official must disclose to the institution any adverse interest of a client — and, specifically, any adverse interest of a client that directly affects a student under his or her direct supervision.
canon-ii-sec-33.w: A teacher grades and mentors students; a client’s interest against a student (or the school) can compromise both roles.

canon-ii-sec-37.x: Online posts must uphold the dignity of the profession and respect for the law — whether the post is public or in a restricted setting that still has an audience.
t: “Friends only” is still an audience: a restricted setting is not a shield.

d.h: A lawyer who posted insulting and threatening statements about a doctor on Facebook was suspended for one year. Posts set to “Friends” were not private: they could be viewed by many and shared further, so there was no reasonable expectation of privacy.
d.r: Social media posts and lawyer discipline; the case behind the “restricted setting” language.

canon-ii-sec-39.x: No creating or running anonymous or fake social media accounts to hide one’s identity in order to get around the law or the CPRA.
t: Anonymity alone is not banned; anonymity for the purpose of circumventing the law or the CPRA is.

canon-ii-sec-41.x: A lawyer who discusses client matters through a social media account must take steps to prevent inadvertent disclosure of, or unauthorized access to, that account.
k: Practical meaning: secure passwords, two-factor authentication, no shared devices, care with group chats.

canon-ii-sec-44.x: Be careful with posts and comments that could create a conflict of interest — for example, publicly taking a position against a current or former client, or commenting on a matter one is handling for the other side.

canon-iii-sec-5.x: A lawyer who appears is presumed authorized; no written power of attorney is needed to appear in court. The court may, on its own or on motion and for just cause, require proof of authority.
t: Contrast Sec. 4: authority to appear is presumed, but authority to compromise or to receive payment of the client’s claim requires a special power of attorney.
This is the former Rule 138, Sec. 21, moved into the CPRA (the CPRA repealed Rule 138, Secs. 20–37).
canon-iii-sec-5.o: Rule 138, Sec. 21 of the Rules of Court

canon-iii-sec-9.x: If a lawyer learns that the client, during the representation, committed fraud on a court, agency or its officer in the matter handled, the lawyer must promptly call on the client to correct it. The fraud also lets the lawyer end the engagement.
k: Step 1: call on the client to rectify.
Step 2 (if the client refuses): the lawyer may terminate.
t: Failing to call on the client to rectify is a light offense (Sec. 35(e)).
The 1988 rule required termination if the client refused; the CPRA makes the fraud a ground the lawyer may invoke.

canon-iii-sec-10.x: A lawyer or firm answers for the mistakes, negligence, acts and omissions of a subordinate lawyer, paralegal or employee under direct supervision and acting within assigned tasks, where they cause damage that dishonors the profession or breach confidentiality. Defense: proof of the diligence of a good parent of a family in selecting and supervising that person.
k: Elements: (1) subordinate under direct supervision and control; (2) acting within assigned tasks; (3) damage or injury that dishonors the profession or violates confidentiality.
Defense: diligence in selection and supervision.
t: The defense mirrors the employer’s defense under Civil Code, Art. 2180 — a useful cross-subject link.

canon-iii-sec-11.x: The supervising lawyer co-signs submissions made with the supervised lawyer, and is liable for the supervised lawyer’s violation if he or she (a) ordered or ratified it, (b) knew of it in time to prevent or mitigate it but did nothing, or (c) should have known in time to take remedial action.
k: (a) orders or ratifies;
(b) knows and fails to act;
(c) should have known — a negligence standard.
Supervising lawyers of law students under Rule 138-A are included.
t: Ground (c) goes further than the U.S. Model Rule 5.1, which stops at actual knowledge.

canon-iii-sec-12.x: Acting on a superior’s instructions is no excuse: a supervised lawyer remains personally bound by the CPRA.
t: “I was only following the partner’s orders” is not a defense.

canon-iii-sec-15.x: A lawyer joining a firm must disclose, as early as possible, former clients who may conflict with the firm’s current clients. Where a potential conflict exists, the new lawyer must not work on the affected client’s case.
t: The CPRA screens the incoming lawyer from the affected case.

canon-iii-sec-18.x: Duties to former clients: (a) keep their confidences after the engagement ends; (b) do not use information from the former representation; (c) do not take on a new client in the same or a related matter whose interests are materially adverse to the former client, unless the former client gives written informed consent.
k: Exceptions to (a) and (b): written informed consent, allowance by the CPRA or law, or the information has become generally known.
Test for (c): same or related matter + materially adverse interests.
t: The duty of confidentiality survives the end of the engagement — and even the client’s death.

Older cases (e.g., Quiambao) put the bar broadly — even against a former client in unrelated cases. Sec. 18(c) now limits it to the same or a related matter with materially adverse interests; the duties in (a) and (b) still apply in every matter.

d.h: A lawyer who had acted for the complainant later appeared against her in other cases for the opposing side. The Court held there was conflict of interest even if no confidential information was used: the rule prevents the appearance of treachery and protects trust in the profession.
d.r: Conflict with a former client; no need to prove use of confidences.

canon-iii-sec-19.x: Representing a corporation or organization does not automatically mean representing its parent, subsidiary or other affiliates. A corporate lawyer who also sits on the board must check whether the two roles conflict and, if they do, disclose the conflict to everyone concerned.
canon-iii-sec-19.w: The organization itself is the client; officers and affiliates are not clients by default.

canon-iii-sec-20.x: A legal services organization is a private body — a legal aid clinic, partnership, association or corporation — whose main purpose is free legal service. The lawyer-client relationship arises only with the handling lawyers, but every lawyer who took part in a matter is bound by the conflict and confidentiality rules.
t: Only the handling lawyers become counsel — so one clinic lawyer’s client does not disqualify unrelated lawyers in the same organization.

canon-iii-sec-23.x: A lawyer may not, without just cause, refuse a court’s or agency’s request to act as amicus curiae in his or her field of expertise.

canon-iii-sec-24.x: Keep up with legal developments; take continuing legal education; support high standards in law schools and student training; help educate the public about the law. IBP chapters provide supervising lawyers to legal aid clinics in their areas.

i.t: Mandatory Continuing Legal Education, B.M. No. 850, as amended
i.s: The units every practising lawyer must complete each compliance period; the duty in Sec. 24 to “participate in continuing legal education programs” is enforced through it.

i.t: Revised Law Student Practice Rule (Rule 138-A), A.M. No. 19-03-24-SC
i.s: Certified law students may give limited legal services and appear in court through a law school clinic, always under a supervising lawyer.

canon-iii-sec-25.x: Lawyers should support internships and apprenticeships, accept law students for training, treat them as junior colleagues and future counsel, and supervise them conscientiously.

canon-iii-sec-26.x: Pay IBP dues promptly unless a law or rule expressly exempts you.
t: Being a senior citizen, working abroad, or not practising does not by itself exempt a lawyer from IBP dues.

i.t: Rule 139-A of the Rules of Court (Integrated Bar of the Philippines)
i.s: Every lawyer is a member of the IBP and pays annual dues. Default for six months warrants suspension of IBP membership; default for one year is a ground to remove the lawyer’s name from the Roll of Attorneys.

d.h: A lawyer who stopped paying IBP dues for years, claiming an exemption as a senior citizen, and who misrepresented his IBP compliance in pleadings, was suspended. Exemption from taxes for senior citizens does not cover IBP dues, which are a condition of practice.

d.n: Letter of Atty. Cecilio Y. Arevalo, Jr. Requesting Exemption from Payment of IBP Dues
d.h: A lawyer who worked abroad and in government and did not practise was denied an exemption: dues are a regulatory measure tied to membership in the Bar, not to actual practice.

canon-iii-sec-29.x: A lawyer who leaves a firm remains bound to keep the confidences of that firm’s clients.

canon-iii-sec-30.x: Within a firm, a lawyer may share a client’s matter with partners, associates, paralegals, interns and staff who are or will be working on it, unless the client forbids it. The lawyer who received the confidences must take measures so that those colleagues do not disclose or use them without the client’s written informed consent.
t: Sharing is limited to people involved in handling the account — not the whole firm.

canon-iii-sec-31.x: Client confidences may not be discussed even with family members.

canon-iii-sec-32.x: A lawyer must not reveal that he or she was consulted about a particular case, except to avoid a possible conflict of interest.
t: Even the fact of a consultation is protected — not only what was said.

canon-iii-sec-33.x: Foreign lawyers may not practise law in the Philippines, directly or indirectly.
t: Rooted in the Constitution: the practice of professions is limited to Filipino citizens save as provided by law (Art. XII, Sec. 14). Admission to the Bar requires citizenship (Rule 138, Sec. 2).

canon-iii-sec-34.x: Lawyers should take part in improving the legal system: law reform, better administration of justice, and advocacy in areas such as the environment, indigenous peoples’ rights, human rights, access to justice and good governance.

canon-iii-sec-36.x: A lawyer appointed counsel de officio may not refuse limited legal services pro bono because of a conflict of interest; instead he or she discloses the conflict to all affected. In any case, the lawyer must render the service to the extent needed to protect the person’s fundamental rights and remedies. Government lawyers are not exempt and may be appointed de officio unless law, Civil Service rules, or a conflict with the government prevents it.
k: Conflict is not a ground to refuse de officio limited services — disclose instead.
Floor: protect fundamental rights and preserve remedies.
Government lawyers can be appointed.
t: This is the reverse of the usual conflict rule: in limited, court-appointed services the duty to protect fundamental rights outweighs the conflict.

i.t: Rules on the Unified Legal Aid Service (ULAS), A.M. No. 22-11-01-SC
i.s: The current framework for compulsory free legal aid by every lawyer; de officio and limited legal services count toward it.

canon-iii-sec-37.x: Confidences received in limited legal services are protected exactly as in a regular engagement.

canon-iii-sec-38.x: Outside the de officio situation in Sec. 36, a lawyer must stop giving limited legal services on becoming aware of an actual or potential conflict, unless the client gives written informed consent. Limited legal services end when the service is completed.

canon-iii-sec-39.x: Limited legal services given by law student practitioners under the Clinical Legal Education Program are governed by the CPRA.

i.t: Revised Law Student Practice Rule (Rule 138-A), A.M. No. 19-03-24-SC
i.s: Certified law students may give limited legal services and appear in court through a law school clinic, always under a supervising lawyer.

canon-iii-sec-40.x: Clinic directors and supervising lawyers under Rule 138-A must give students meaningful training, take responsibility for the students’ work while under supervision, and follow the law student practice rules.

i.t: Revised Law Student Practice Rule (Rule 138-A), A.M. No. 19-03-24-SC
i.s: Certified law students may give limited legal services and appear in court through a law school clinic, always under a supervising lawyer.

canon-iii-sec-42.x: On a referral, with the client’s written informed consent, the referring lawyer may share in the fee in proportion to the work done and responsibility assumed. A lawyer who completes a deceased lawyer’s unfinished business may share fees with the deceased lawyer’s heirs or estate.
t: No pure “referral fee” for doing nothing: the share follows work and responsibility.
Sharing fees with a non-lawyer is a less serious offense (Sec. 34(o)); the heirs of a deceased lawyer are the recognized exception.

canon-iii-sec-44.x: No fee, commission, rebate or other compensation from anyone other than the client without the client’s written informed consent. Even with consent, third-party payment must not affect the lawyer’s independence, judgment or loyalty, and must not lead to disclosure of privileged information.
k: Typical case: an employer or insurer pays for the lawyer of an employee or insured.
Three safeguards: consent, independence, privilege.

canon-iii-sec-45.x: A lawyer is entitled to prompt payment. If there is no express fee agreement, the lawyer is paid reasonable fees under the Sec. 41 factors (quantum meruit).

canon-iii-sec-46.x: Avoid fee disputes with clients; sue only to prevent imposition, injustice or fraud.

canon-iii-sec-48.x: Where the law provides funds, the court may order a counsel de officio paid an amount it fixes using the Sec. 41 factors — unless the work falls under limited legal services.
t: Discretionary (“may”), and subject to available funds.
canon-iii-sec-48.o: Rule 138, Sec. 32 of the Rules of Court (now repealed and absorbed)

canon-iii-sec-55.x: The death of the lawyer or of the client ends the lawyer-client relationship. But a lawyer’s death does not end the engagement between the client and the law firm handling the matter.
t: When a party-client dies, counsel must inform the court within thirty days and give the name and address of the legal representative (Rules of Court, Rule 3, Sec. 16).
Contrast: the firm survives the death of one of its lawyers.

canon-iii-sec-56.x: When the engagement ends, the lawyer — subject to the attorney’s lien — must at once account for and turn over the client’s documents, evidence, funds and property, and cooperate with the successor lawyer. The lawyer has a retaining lien on the client’s funds, documents and papers lawfully in his or her possession until fair fees and disbursements are paid, and may apply those funds to them.
k: Retaining lien (this section): over client’s funds, documents and papers in the lawyer’s possession.
Charging lien (Sec. 54): over money judgments and executions in the case.
t: The lien is not a license to hold documents the client urgently needs to protect rights in pending litigation; the duty to cooperate with successor counsel stays.

canon-iv-sec-2.x: Take on only what you can deliver. With the client’s prior written consent, a lawyer may bring in collaborating counsel.

canon-iv-sec-4.x: Be diligent in every undertaking and do not cause delay. Come to trial knowing the law, the facts and the evidence, and ready with object and documentary evidence and the witnesses’ judicial affidavits when required.

i.t: Judicial Affidavit Rule, A.M. No. 12-8-8-SC (2012)
i.s: Judicial affidavits replace direct testimony in most cases and must be filed before the pre-trial or preliminary conference.

canon-iv-sec-5.x: After reasonable inquiry, give the client a prompt and objective assessment of the merits and likely outcome, and explain the viable options so the client can decide.
t: Neither overstating nor understating the case — false hope to win an engagement is a violation.

canon-iv-sec-7.x: Avoid asking for extensions unless the rules allow them or there is good cause. Once an extension is granted, file within it — unless the client has decided not to pursue the case or there is other justifiable cause.
t: Under the 2019 amendments to the Rules of Civil Procedure, a defendant gets only one extension of up to thirty days to answer (Rule 11, Sec. 11).
Letting an extended period lapse is a classic neglect case.

canon-iv-sec-9.x: A lawyer who also practises another profession (e.g., accountancy, brokerage) must state in the contract what services he or she is engaged to perform, and the other profession must not compromise the lawyer’s competence, integrity, probity or independence.
canon-iv-sec-9.w: The client must know when the lawyer is acting as lawyer — privilege and professional duties depend on it.

canon-iv-sec-10.x: A lawyer in business or another non-legal profession is still bound by the CPRA’s ethical duties.
t: Discipline reaches conduct outside the practice of law: the lawyer’s fitness is judged as a whole.

canon-v-sec-2.x: With a client from a vulnerable sector, the lawyer must be sensitive to the client’s circumstances and the special laws that apply, give a higher standard of service, and assert the client’s right to meaningful access to justice. A vulnerable person is one at higher risk of harm — including children, the elderly, the homeless, persons with disability, persons deprived of liberty, human rights victims, victims of domestic violence or armed conflict, the socio-economically disadvantaged, racial or ethnic minorities, and those with debilitating conditions.
k: Special laws to keep in mind: R.A. 7610 (children), R.A. 9262 (VAWC), R.A. 9344 (juvenile justice), R.A. 7277 as amended (persons with disability).
t: The list is inclusive (“shall include”), not exhaustive.

canon-v-sec-4.x: Same standard of service for every client whatever the pay — except the higher standard owed to vulnerable persons.
t: Pro bono and de officio clients get the same diligence as paying clients.

canon-vi-sec-3.x: The complaint must be verified, state the acts or omissions clearly and concisely, and come with the witnesses’ judicial affidavits and supporting documents. If filed with the IBP, six copies go to the IBP Secretary or a chapter secretary, who transmits it to the Board of Governors.
t: Judicial affidavits are attached at the outset — a change from the old practice under Rule 139-B.
canon-vi-sec-3.o: Rule 139-B of the Rules of Court (repealed by the CPRA)

canon-vi-sec-4.x: The IBP recommends 150 lawyers in good standing, drawn proportionately from its nine regions, to serve as Investigating Commissioners; only those the Supreme Court approves may serve, for three-year terms, and each takes an oath.
canon-vi-sec-4.w: The Supreme Court controls who investigates lawyers — consistent with its exclusive constitutional power over the practice of law (Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)).

canon-vi-sec-5.x: The IBP Board of Governors assigns a complaint by raffle to one Investigating Commissioner — or, in special circumstances, to a panel of three.

canon-vi-sec-6.x: For a complaint against a government lawyer, the Investigating Commissioner decides within five calendar days from raffle whether the agency, the Ombudsman, or the Supreme Court has jurisdiction. The case proceeds if it touches the lawyer’s continuing duties under the CPRA, or if the allegations, if true, would make the lawyer unfit to practise; otherwise dismissal is recommended.
k: Test: does the charge concern the lawyer qua lawyer (continuing CPRA duties / fitness to practise) or only the official qua official?
t: Read with Sec. 2: a complaint seeking to discipline a government lawyer as a member of the Bar is filed only with the Supreme Court.

canon-vi-sec-7.x: An Investigating Commissioner must recuse for relationship within the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity with a party or counsel, a professional legal relationship, pecuniary interest, or having acted as counsel for a party (this last one can be waived by the parties’ written consent on record). A motion to disqualify goes to the IBP Board, which resolves it within five calendar days; its ruling is final.
t: Only the “acted as counsel” ground can be waived by written consent.
The text says the Board designates “a replace” of the commissioner — so it reads in both the primary and the ChanRobles transcriptions; the intended word is “replacement”.

canon-vi-sec-8.x: The Investigating Commissioner investigates and submits a report with recommendations to the IBP Board within 180 calendar days from raffle — the overall ceiling for the investigation.

canon-vi-sec-9.x: Only three submissions are allowed: complaint, answer, and position papers — all verified. The complaint carries a certificate of non-forum shopping. An unverified complaint is recommended for outright dismissal; an unverified answer or position paper is disregarded.
t: Different consequences: unverified complaint → dismissal; unverified answer/position paper → not considered.

canon-vi-sec-10.x: Prohibited: motions to dismiss (except for lack of jurisdiction, litis pendentia or res judicata); bills of particulars; motions to reopen or for new trial; petitions for relief from judgment; supplemental pleadings; and motions for reconsideration of a judgment on the merits (but reconsideration of interlocutory orders is allowed).
t: The pattern copies summary procedure — speed is the design goal.
Note the reversal from ordinary civil procedure: here an MR of an interlocutory order is allowed, an MR of the judgment on the merits is not.

canon-vi-sec-11.x: Within fifteen calendar days from raffle, if there is no prima facie showing of liability, the commissioner recommends outright dismissal to the Supreme Court, which may adopt it; otherwise the Court orders further proceedings.
t: Only the Supreme Court dismisses — the commissioner only recommends.

canon-vi-sec-12.x: No disciplinary case may be started against a dead lawyer; one filed anyway is dismissed; and a lawyer’s death while the case is pending also causes its dismissal.
canon-vi-sec-12.w: Discipline protects the public and the courts from an unfit practitioner; a deceased lawyer no longer practises, so the case becomes pointless.

canon-vi-sec-13.x: Within fifteen calendar days from raffle, the commissioner issues summons, with the verified complaint and supporting documents, requiring a verified answer.

canon-vi-sec-14.x: The verified answer, with judicial affidavits and supporting documents, is due within thirty calendar days from receipt of summons. One fifteen-day extension may be given, on motion and for good cause. Two copies go to the commissioner, with proof of service on the complainant.
t: Only one extension, and only fifteen days.

canon-vi-sec-15.x: If the verified answer shows the complaint has no merit, the commissioner recommends dismissal to the Supreme Court; otherwise the Court directs further proceedings.

canon-vi-sec-17.x: The IBP Board may appoint a member of the Bar as counsel de officio for the complainant or the respondent when assistance is needed.

canon-vi-sec-18.x: Once issues are joined (or the respondent fails to answer), the investigation proceeds — ex parte if the respondent, despite notice, does not answer or appear — and always with dispatch. The respondent has full opportunity to be heard, with or without counsel, and to present witnesses. The commissioner may issue subpoenas and administer oaths.

canon-vi-sec-19.x: Wilful disobedience of the commissioner’s subpoena or lawful order is indirect contempt. Show cause within ten days; a hearing (if needed) ends within fifteen days; the report goes to the IBP Board within fifteen days; the Board acts within thirty days and its action is immediately executory. Appeal lies to the Supreme Court, but execution is stayed only by a bond fixed by the Board.
k: 10 days — show cause
15 days — hearing
15 days — report
30 days — Board resolution
Appeal to SC; stay only on bond

canon-vi-sec-20.x: On receipt of the answer, the commissioner notifies the parties to file, simultaneously and within ten non-extendible calendar days, preliminary conference briefs containing admissions, stipulations, issues, judicial affidavits and marked exhibits (with counsel’s certification of faithful reproduction), and other matters that help speed the case.

canon-vi-sec-21.x: Within ten calendar days from receipt of the briefs, the commissioner issues a Preliminary Conference Order summarizing stipulated facts, issues and exhibits, and directs verified position papers within ten non-extendible days.

canon-vi-sec-22.x: Within ten calendar days from the last position paper, the commissioner decides whether a clarificatory hearing is needed; if so, it is set within fifteen days, limited to the factual issues identified, may be in person or by videoconference, and ends within thirty days. The commissioner questions the witnesses first; the parties may then confront them on those issues.
t: It is a clarificatory hearing, not a full trial: the commissioner sets the issues and leads the questioning.

canon-vi-sec-23.x: Proceedings before the IBP are recorded.

canon-vi-sec-24.x: A party who does not appear at the clarificatory hearing waives the right to take part in it.

canon-vi-sec-25.x: The report and recommendation is due within sixty non-extendible calendar days from the last position paper (if there is no hearing) or within thirty non-extendible days from the end of the hearing. It attaches the transcript, audio recording, or the commissioner’s signed notes, and the evidence; it need not wait for the transcription. Videoconference hearings are recorded and form part of the record.
k: No hearing → 60 days from last position paper.
With hearing → 30 days from end of hearing.

canon-vi-sec-26.x: The IBP Board has ninety non-extendible calendar days from receipt of the report to submit to the Supreme Court its resolution adopting, modifying or disapproving it.
t: The Board’s resolution is still only a recommendation: the Supreme Court alone imposes discipline (a change made by B.M. No. 1645 in 2015 and kept by the CPRA).

canon-vi-sec-27.x: Depositions may be taken under the Rules of Civil Procedure, with the commissioner’s leave.

canon-vi-sec-28.x: Filing and service may be personal, by registered mail, accredited courier, e-mail or other electronic means, or under international conventions. The office and e-mail addresses the lawyer gave the IBP are the official addresses for service.
t: A lawyer who never updates his or her IBP addresses cannot complain of not receiving notices sent there.

canon-vi-sec-29.x: Substantial defects in the complaint, notices, answer, proceedings or report that may cause a miscarriage of justice are raised as errors before the Supreme Court. If the defect amounts to denial of due process, the remedy is a motion to reopen before the IBP Board within sixty calendar days from knowledge.

canon-vi-sec-30.x: For cases the Supreme Court starts itself or that are filed with it, the Court may refer the case to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the IBP, or another fact-finding body. Referred cases follow Sections 5 to 29, and the Court reviews the report directly.

canon-vi-sec-31.x: After the answer (or the lapse of the period to answer), the Supreme Court — on its own or on recommendation of the IBP Board, the Bar Confidant or the fact-finding body — may preventively suspend the lawyer for up to 180 calendar days, or until lifted, to prevent obstruction, tampering with evidence, or intimidation of witnesses.
k: When: after answer or lapse of period to answer.
Who: only the Supreme Court.
Why: to protect the investigation, not to punish.
How long: up to 180 days or until lifted.
t: Preventive suspension is not a penalty.
canon-vi-sec-31.o: Rule 139-B, Sec. 15 (which had no fixed limit)

canon-vi-sec-34.x: The less serious offenses: simple misconduct; simple negligence (not depriving the client of a day in court); violating Supreme Court rules on bar matters and disciplinary cases, including wilful disobedience of SC or IBP orders; simple dishonesty; other conflict-of-interest violations; prohibited borrowing from or lending to a client; other unlawful threats; frivolous suits (once finally so declared); violating sub judice; deliberately not paying just debts; withdrawing without good cause and written notice; intemperate language before a tribunal; unjustified refusal to account for client funds; sharing fees with non-lawyers; and other reportorial violations.
k: Pair each with its serious version in Sec. 33: simple vs. gross misconduct; simple vs. gross negligence; simple vs. serious dishonesty; “other” vs. intentional conflict-of-interest violations; other threats vs. threats amounting to a crime.
t: The dividing line for negligence: did it deprive the client of his or her day in court? If yes — serious (Sec. 33(d)).
Frivolous suits count only after a final decision dismissing them as frivolous.

canon-vi-sec-35.x: The light offenses: violating IBP membership rules; vulgar or offensive language in personal dealings; fraternizing with court or agency personnel where one has a pending case, so as to suggest influence; frivolous motions for inhibition; failing to promptly call on a client to rectify fraud; and other similar infractions.
t: Offensive language before a tribunal is less serious (Sec. 34(m)); in personal dealings it is light (Sec. 35(b)).

canon-vi-sec-36.x: A lawyer who knowingly helps another lawyer commit any CPRA offense may also be held liable.

canon-vi-sec-41.x: Fines must be paid, and client money or property returned, within three months from receipt of the decision; otherwise the Court may cite the lawyer for indirect contempt.
t: Restitution of client money is ordered in the disciplinary case itself when the amounts are intrinsically linked to the professional engagement.

canon-vi-sec-42.x: A lawyer already disbarred who is found guilty of a new charge may be fined or ordered to return a client’s money or property. If the new offense deserves disbarment or suspension, that penalty is not imposed (there is nothing left to take away) but is recorded in the lawyer’s file at the Office of the Bar Confidant — and counted against any later petition for judicial clemency.
t: There is no “double disbarment” — but the record matters at clemency.

canon-vi-sec-44.x: Proceedings against lawyers are confidential; only the Supreme Court’s final order is published like its other decisions.
t: Confidentiality binds the parties: a complainant who publicizes the complaint risks contempt.
canon-vi-sec-44.w: To let the Court investigate free from outside pressure, to protect lawyers’ reputations against baseless charges, and to keep the press from trying the case first.

d.h: Lawyers who distributed copies of a pending disbarment complaint to the media were held in indirect contempt for violating the confidentiality of disciplinary proceedings. The media outlets were not held liable: they reported a matter of public interest (the Maguindanao massacre case) and the respondent lawyer had become a public figure in it.

canon-vi-sec-46.x: The sworn statement (Sec. 45) is proof of compliance with the suspension, and the lawyer may resume practice once it is filed with the Supreme Court. A false statement is a ground for disbarment; if the Bar Confidant finds one, it refers it to the Court within five days.
t: Resumption is upon filing — no separate order lifting the suspension is needed.

d.h: The Court laid down the earlier guidelines: suspension is not automatically lifted at the end of the period; the lawyer files a sworn statement of non-practice, with copies to the courts where he or she has pending cases, and a false statement is ground for more severe punishment.
d.r: The pre-CPRA procedure that Secs. 45–46 build on.

canon-vi-sec-49.x: The Supreme Court first evaluates a clemency petition for prima facie merit under the Sec. 48 criteria. With merit, it refers the petition to the Bar Confidant or a fact-finding body; without merit, it denies it outright.

canon-vi-sec-50.x: The Bar Confidant or designated body finishes its investigation and reports within ninety calendar days from referral.

canon-vi-sec-51.x: Judicial clemency is decided on clear and convincing evidence.
t: Contrast Sec. 32: discipline needs only substantial evidence; reinstatement after disbarment needs clear and convincing proof of reform. The higher bar is on the lawyer seeking to return.

canon-vi-sec-53.x: Reasonable and necessary expenses of disciplinary and disbarment proceedings may be charged to the parties as costs, upon proof.

gp-sec-3.x: The CPRA takes effect fifteen calendar days after publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. It was published in the Manila Bulletin and the Philippine Star on May 14, 2023, and took effect on May 29, 2023, according to OCA Circular No. 200-2023 (one later Supreme Court resolution, A.M. No. 23-05-05-SC, gives May 30).
t: Approved April 11, 2023 in Baguio City; launched April 13, 2023; effective May 29, 2023.

i.t: OCA Circular No. 200-2023
i.s: Informed first- and second-level courts of the CPRA and of its effectivity on May 29, 2023, after publication on May 14, 2023.
